title: Tallies & Picture Graphs
blurb: Counting with tally marks bundled in fives, collecting the counts into a table with a total, drawing picture graphs and block graphs one-for-one, and answering most, fewest, how-many-more and altogether questions from them.

lessons.title: Tally Marks
lessons.concreteComparison: Counting a flock as it comes through the gate is hard — the animals do not wait while you remember where you were. A tally solves it: one mark per animal, and every fifth mark laid across the last four to close a bundle.
lessons.objective: Record a count with tally marks bundled in fives, read a tally back as a number, and say why the bundles make counting reliable.
concept: **One mark for each thing.** A tally records as you go, so you never have to hold the running total in your head. That is what makes it work while the sheep are still moving.

**Every fifth mark closes a bundle.** Four upright marks, then the fifth laid across them. Bundles of five can be counted in fives instead of ones, so a long tally is read quickly and without losing your place.

**Read it as fives and singles.** Two bundles and two singles is $2 \times 5 + 2 = 12$. Count the bundles first, then add the leftovers — and there can never be five leftovers, because the fifth would have closed a new bundle.
lessons.keyIdea: A tally records one mark per thing and closes a bundle every fifth mark, so the count can be read back in fives.

facts.title: Reading a tally
facts.explanation: Two bundles of five and two singles make twelve.

facts.title: Never five singles
facts.explanation: A fifth single would close a bundle, so at most four are ever left over.

workedExamples.statement: A tally shows one bundle of five and two singles. What is the count?
workedExamples.solution: One bundle is $1 \times 5 = 5$, and two singles add $2$: the count is $5 + 2 = 7$.

workedExamples.statement: Draw $12$ as tally marks. How many bundles and how many singles?
workedExamples.note: How many fives fit into twelve?
workedExamples.solution: Two whole bundles use $2 \times 5 = 10$ marks, leaving $12 - 10 = 2$ singles. So the tally is two bundles and two singles — and $2$ is less than $5$, as it must be.

commonMistakes.text: Leaving five singles standing instead of closing a bundle.
commonMistakes.correction: The fifth mark goes ACROSS the other four and closes the bundle. If you can see five uprights, one of them should have been laid across.

commonMistakes.text: Counting the bundles as the answer — reading two bundles and two singles as 4.
commonMistakes.correction: Each bundle is worth five, not one: 2 × 5 + 2 = 12. Counting bundles alone throws away four fifths of the count.

tryIt.statement: A tally shows three bundles and one single. What is the count?
Draw $9$ as tally marks and say how many singles are left over.
tryIt.solution: One bundle uses $5$ marks, leaving $9 - 5 = 4$ singles. Four is the most that can ever be left, since a fifth would close another bundle.

steps.title: One mark, one animal
beats: Counting a moving flock in your head fails, because the animals do not wait. A tally records instead: one mark for each animal as it passes.
The picture below shows a tally of $7$ sheep — one closed bundle of five, and two more standing on their own.
The fifth mark of every bundle is laid ACROSS the other four. That is what turns a long row of marks into something you can read at a glance.

steps.title: Read the tally
steps.intro: Count the bundles, then the singles.

examples.prompt: One bundle and two singles. What is the count?
steps: Two singles add $2$: the count is $5 + 2 = 7$.

examples.prompt: Three bundles and one single. What is the count?

steps.title: What does the tally say?
steps.intro: Bundles are worth five each.

problems.prompt: The tally below shows:
problems.explanation: Two bundles are $2 \times 5 = 10$, plus two singles: $10 + 2 = 12$. Counting the bundles and singles as one each would give only $4$.

problems.prompt: Two bundles and four singles is:
problems.explanation: $2 \times 5 = 10$ from the bundles, plus $4$: $10 + 4 = 14$. Four singles is the most there can ever be.

problems.prompt: A tally of one bundle and no singles is:
problems.explanation: A closed bundle is worth five marks: $1 \times 5 = 5$.

steps.title: Why bundle at all?
steps.prompt: What do the bundles of five make easier?
options: reading a long tally back quickly
steps.explanation: The marks are the same either way, but bundles can be counted in fives: $1 \times 5 = 5$, then add the singles. Reading two bundles and two singles as $10 + 2 = 12$ is far faster and safer than counting twelve separate strokes.

steps.title: Tallies are older than writing
steps.body: Notched bones tens of thousands of years old carry marks grouped in small bundles — the same idea you have just used, from before anyone had numerals to write down. Whoever cut them had worked out that counting things one at a time is unreliable, and that grouping fixes it.

steps.title: Drawing a tally from a number
beats: Going the other way, from a number to a tally, asks how many whole bundles of five fit inside it.
For $12$: two bundles use $2 \times 5 = 10$ marks, and $12 - 10 = 2$ are left as singles — exactly what the picture below shows.
There can never be five singles. The fifth would be laid across the other four and become a bundle, so the leftovers are always $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$ or $4$.

steps.title: Draw the tally
steps.intro: How many fives fit, and what is left?

examples.prompt: Draw $12$ as tally marks.
steps: Two bundles and two singles — and $2 < 5$ ✓.

examples.prompt: Draw $9$ as tally marks.
steps: Left over: $9 - 5 = 4$ singles — the most possible.

steps.title: From number to tally
steps.intro: Fill whole bundles first.

problems.prompt: $17$ as tally marks is:
problems.explanation: $3 \times 5 = 15$, leaving $17 - 15 = 2$ singles. Seven singles could never stand — five of them would have closed another bundle.

problems.prompt: The most singles a tally can ever show is:
problems.explanation: A fifth single is laid across the other four and closes a bundle, so at most four stand alone: $5 - 5 = 0$ left standing.

problems.prompt: $10$ as tally marks is:
problems.explanation: $2 \times 5 = 10$ exactly, so both bundles close and nothing is left: $10 - 10 = 0$ singles.

steps.title: The impossible tally
steps.prompt: A tally shows one bundle and five singles. What is wrong?
options: the fifth single should have closed a second bundle
there should be no singles at all
bundles cannot be drawn beside singles
steps.explanation: The fifth mark is always laid across the other four, so five singles can never stand: at most four do. The count is $1 \times 5 + 5 = 10$, which should have been drawn as two closed bundles.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A tally records one mark per thing, as you go.
Every fifth mark is laid across the other four to close a bundle.
Read a tally as bundles then singles: $2 \times 5 + 2 = 12$.
There are never five singles — at most four are left standing.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: When reading a tally, touch each bundle and count "five, ten, fifteen" out loud before you add the singles. Counting the bundles in ones is the mistake that costs four fifths of the answer.

steps.title: Chapter practice
steps.intro: Bundles of five, then the leftovers.

problems.prompt: Four bundles and three singles is:
problems.explanation: $4 \times 5 = 20$ from the bundles, plus $3$: $20 + 3 = 23$.

problems.prompt: $8$ as tally marks is:
problems.explanation: One bundle uses $5$, leaving $8 - 5 = 3$ singles.

problems.prompt: A tally of three bundles and no singles is:
problems.explanation: $3 \times 5 = 15$. Counting the bundles as one each gives $3$ — the classic error.

steps.title: You've finished "Tally Marks"
steps.body: You can now record a count that is happening too fast to hold in your head. The next lesson collects several of those counts side by side, where they can finally be compared.

lessons.title: Making a Table
lessons.concreteComparison: Three tallies scattered across a page tell you three things separately. Put them in a table, one row each, and a fourth thing appears that no single tally could show — which is the biggest.
lessons.objective: Collect several counts into a table, find the total, and use the total as a check on the individual counts.
concept: **A table gives each count its own row.** Sheep $7$, goats $12$, horses $5$. Written in a column, the counts line up and can be compared at a glance — which no scattered tally can do.
**The total is the sum of the rows.** $7 + 12 + 5 = 24$ animals altogether. It is worth writing down even when nobody asked for it, because it is a check on everything above it.
**A missing row can be found from the total.** If the total is $24$ and two rows read $7$ and $12$, the third must be $24 - 19 = 5$. The total and the rows hold each other honest.
lessons.keyIdea: A table lines counts up so they can be compared, and its total is both a summary and a check.

facts.title: The total
facts.explanation: The rows add to the total number of animals.

facts.title: A missing row
facts.explanation: Total minus the known rows gives the one that is missing.

workedExamples.statement: A herder counts $7$ sheep, $12$ goats and $5$ horses. Make the table and find the total.
workedExamples.note: One row per kind, then add.
workedExamples.solution: Three rows: sheep $7$, goats $12$, horses $5$. The total is $7 + 12 + 5 = 24$ animals. Lined up like that, it is immediately clear that goats are the most numerous, which the three separate tallies never showed.

workedExamples.statement: A table shows sheep $7$, goats $12$ and a smudged third row. The total is $24$. What was the third row?
workedExamples.solution: The two readable rows come to $7 + 12 = 19$, and the total is $24$, so the missing row is $24 - 19 = 5$. Check: $19 + 5 = 24$ ✓.

commonMistakes.text: Writing the counts down without a total, so nothing can be checked afterwards.
commonMistakes.correction: The total is the table's receipt. Without it, a wrong row can sit there forever; with it, the rows and the total have to agree.

commonMistakes.text: Adding the total into itself when finding a missing row.
commonMistakes.correction: The total is not a row. Add only the rows — 7 + 12 = 19 — and subtract that from the total: 24 − 19 = 5.

tryIt.statement: A table reads red $6$, blue $9$, green $4$. Find the total and say which colour is most common.
tryIt.solution: $6 + 9 + 4 = 19$ altogether. Blue is the most common at $9$, ahead of red by $9 - 6 = 3$.

tryIt.statement: A table has rows of $8$ and $6$, and a total of $20$. What is the missing row?
tryIt.solution: The known rows come to $8 + 6 = 14$, so the missing one is $20 - 14 = 6$. Check: $14 + 6 = 20$ ✓.

steps.title: Counts side by side
beats: Three tallies on three corners of a page tell you three separate things. Bring them into a table — one row each — and they line up.
The picture below shows the three counts together: sheep $7$, goats $12$, horses $5$.
Now a new fact is visible that no single tally could show: goats are the most numerous, beating the sheep by $12 - 7 = 5$. Comparison is what a table is FOR.

steps.title: Build the table
steps.intro: One row per kind, lined up.

examples.prompt: Sheep $7$, goats $12$, horses $5$. Which is the most numerous, and by how much over the sheep?
steps: Lined up, the largest row is the goats at $12$.

examples.prompt: Red $6$, blue $9$, green $4$. Which is fewest, and by how much under the blue?
steps: The smallest row is green at $4$.

steps.title: Read the table
steps.intro: Compare the rows against each other.

problems.prompt: Sheep $7$, goats $12$, horses $5$. The most numerous is:
problems.explanation: $12$ is the largest of the three rows, ahead of the sheep by $12 - 7 = 5$ and the horses by $12 - 5 = 7$.

problems.prompt: With rows of $6$, $9$ and $4$, how many more of the largest than the smallest?
problems.explanation: Largest $9$, smallest $4$: $9 - 4 = 5$ more. The $19$ is the total of all three, a different question.

problems.prompt: The row with the SMALLEST count in sheep $7$, goats $12$, horses $5$ is:
problems.explanation: $5$ is the smallest of the three, below the sheep by $7 - 5 = 2$.

steps.title: What a table adds
steps.prompt: What can a table show that three separate tallies cannot?
options: the exact number in each count
nothing — it is the same information
steps.explanation: Each tally already gives its own number. What the table adds is COMPARISON: lined up, $12 > 7 > 5$ is visible at a glance, and the gap $12 - 7 = 5$ can be read off directly.

steps.title: Why the total goes at the bottom
steps.body: Accountants have written the total under the column for centuries, and the reason is checking rather than tidiness: to verify the work you add the column again and see whether you land on the same number. A total sitting at the bottom is an invitation to check, and that is exactly what it is for.

steps.title: The total, and the missing row
beats: Every table deserves a total. For sheep $7$ and goats $12$ — the picture below — the two rows come to $7 + 12 = 19$.
Add the horses and the whole table totals $7 + 12 + 5 = 24$ animals. Write it down even when nobody asked: it is the table's receipt.
And it works backwards. If the total is $24$ and one row is smudged, the missing count is $24 - 19 = 5$. The rows and the total keep each other honest.

steps.title: Total and missing rows
steps.intro: Rows add to the total; the total finds a row.

examples.prompt: Sheep $7$, goats $12$, horses $5$. What is the total?
Rows of $7$ and $12$, total $24$. What is the missing row?

steps.title: Totals and gaps
steps.intro: Add the rows; subtract to find one.

problems.prompt: Rows of $6$, $9$ and $4$ total:
problems.explanation: $6 + 9 = 15$, then $15 + 4 = 19$. Stopping at $15$ leaves the green row out.

problems.prompt: Two rows read $8$ and $6$, and the total is $20$. The missing row is:
problems.explanation: $8 + 6 = 14$, so the missing row is $20 - 14 = 6$. The $14$ is the two known rows, not the missing one.

problems.prompt: A table's rows add to $22$ but the written total says $24$. This means:
options: something is wrong — they must agree
problems.explanation: The rows and the total have to match; a gap of $24 - 22 = 2$ means a row or the total is wrong. That is exactly why the total is worth writing down.

steps.title: Using the total backwards
steps.prompt: A table has rows of $9$ and $7$ and a total of $20$. The missing row is:
steps.explanation: The known rows come to $9 + 7 = 16$, so the missing one is $20 - 16 = 4$. Check: $16 + 4 = 20$ ✓ — the $16$ is what is already accounted for, not what is missing.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A table gives each count its own row so the counts can be compared.
The total is the sum of the rows: $7 + 12 + 5 = 24$.
Write the total down even when nobody asks — it is the table's check.
A missing row is the total minus the rows you have: $24 - 19 = 5$.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Add your table's rows twice, the second time from the bottom up. Two agreeing totals is far stronger evidence than one, and it costs a few seconds.

steps.title: Chapter practice
steps.intro: Rows, total, and the gap between rows.

problems.prompt: Rows of $5$, $8$ and $3$ total:
In rows of $5$, $8$ and $3$, the largest beats the smallest by:
problems.explanation: $8 - 3 = 5$. The $16$ is the total of all three rows.

problems.prompt: Rows of $10$ and $6$ with a total of $21$ leave a missing row of:
problems.explanation: $10 + 6 = 16$, so the missing row is $21 - 16 = 5$; check $16 + 5 = 21$ ✓.

steps.title: You've finished "Making a Table"
steps.body: A table makes counts comparable, but you still have to read the numbers to compare them. The next lesson draws them instead — and the comparison becomes something you can see without reading at all.

lessons.title: Picture Graphs
lessons.concreteComparison: A table says goats $12$, sheep $7$. A picture graph draws twelve little goats and seven little sheep — and now nobody has to read a number to see which row is longer. The comparison has become a length.
lessons.objective: Read a picture graph where one picture stands for one thing, draw one from a table, and answer comparison questions from the rows.
concept: **One picture stands for one thing.** Six horses drawn means six horses counted. Every row has one picture per animal, which is what makes the row lengths honest.

**Longer rows mean bigger counts.** The horse row at $6$ is longer than the sheep row at $4$, so there are $6 - 4 = 2$ more horses. You can see it before you count it, which is the point of drawing the data at all.
**Every row must start in the same place.** If one row begins further along than another, its length lies about its count. Line the rows up at the left and the picture tells the truth.
lessons.keyIdea: In a picture graph one picture is one thing, so the length of a row IS its count — provided every row starts from the same line.

facts.title: One for one
facts.explanation: Six horses against four sheep: two more, and the row is two longer.

facts.title: Rows total the whole
facts.explanation: Adding the rows gives the total number of animals drawn.

workedExamples.statement: A picture graph shows $6$ horses, $4$ sheep and $3$ camels, one picture each. How many more horses than sheep, and how many animals altogether?
workedExamples.note: Compare the rows, then add them.
workedExamples.solution: Horses beat sheep by $6 - 4 = 2$. Altogether the rows come to $6 + 4 + 3 = 13$ animals. The horse row is the longest, which is visible without counting a single picture.

workedExamples.statement: Monday $5$ and Tuesday $8$ are drawn one picture per visitor. Which row is longer, and by how much?
workedExamples.note: One picture per visitor means the row length is the count.
workedExamples.solution: Tuesday's row is longer, because $8 > 5$. It is $8 - 5 = 3$ pictures longer, which is exactly $3$ more visitors — one picture, one visitor.

commonMistakes.text: Reading a row's length as its count when the rows do not start in line.
commonMistakes.correction: A row that begins further along looks longer than it is. Every row must start from the same left-hand line, or the picture misleads even though every count is right.

commonMistakes.text: Answering "how many more" with the bigger row's count instead of the difference.
commonMistakes.correction: "How many more horses than sheep" asks for the gap: 6 − 4 = 2, not 6. The bigger count answers a different question.

tryIt.statement: A picture graph shows $7$ birds and $3$ fish. How many more birds, and how many creatures altogether?
Why must every row of a picture graph start from the same line?
tryIt.solution: Because the row's LENGTH is what a reader compares. A row starting further along looks longer than its count deserves, so a row of $4$ could appear to beat a row of $6$ even though $6 > 4$.

steps.title: Drawing the count
beats: The graph below draws the animals instead of listing them: $6$ horses, $4$ sheep, $3$ camels — one picture for each animal counted.
That one-for-one rule is what makes the rows honest. Six pictures means six animals, so the LENGTH of the row is the count.
Now the comparison needs no reading at all. The horse row is visibly the longest, and it beats the sheep row by $6 - 4 = 2$.

steps.title: Read the rows
steps.intro: One picture is one thing.

examples.prompt: $6$ horses and $4$ sheep. How many more horses?
$6$ horses, $4$ sheep, $3$ camels. How many animals altogether?

steps.title: Read the picture graph
steps.intro: Row length is the count.

problems.prompt: From the graph below, how many more horses than camels?
problems.explanation: Horses $6$, camels $3$: the gap is $6 - 3 = 3$. The $9$ adds the rows instead of comparing them.

problems.prompt: A row of $8$ pictures against a row of $5$. The longer row has:
problems.explanation: $8 - 5 = 3$ more — and because one picture is one thing, the row is also three pictures longer.

problems.prompt: In a one-for-one picture graph, a row of $7$ pictures means:
problems.explanation: One picture stands for one thing, so seven pictures is seven things — no key to apply and no multiplying to do.

steps.title: What the row length means
steps.prompt: In a one-for-one picture graph, why is the longest row the biggest count?
options: each picture is one thing, so length is the count
because longer rows are drawn first
it is not — you must count every picture
because the rows are always sorted
steps.explanation: One picture per thing means the row length and the count are the same number: $6$ horses draw a row of $6$, beating $4$ sheep by $6 - 4 = 2$ both in count and in length.

steps.title: The first graphs were drawn to argue
steps.body: Picture graphs became popular when people realised a drawing persuades faster than a column of numbers — a nurse called Florence Nightingale famously drew her hospital data to win an argument about sanitation, and won it. Drawing data is not decoration; it is how a count gets noticed.

steps.title: Starting from the same line
beats: The graph below compares two days: Monday $5$ and Tuesday $8$, one picture per visitor.
Tuesday's row is longer, by $8 - 5 = 3$ pictures — which is exactly $3$ more visitors, because each picture is one visitor.

But all of this depends on the rows starting from the SAME line. Let one row begin further along and its length no longer matches its count: a row of $4$ could sit further right and appear to beat a row of $6$. Line them up on the left, always.

steps.title: Compare two rows
steps.intro: Same starting line, then compare lengths.

examples.prompt: Monday $5$, Tuesday $8$. Which day was busier, and by how much?
Monday $5$ and Tuesday $8$. How many visitors over the two days?

steps.title: Fair comparisons
steps.intro: Do the rows start in line?

problems.prompt: Monday $5$, Tuesday $8$. Over both days there were:
problems.explanation: Adding the rows: $5 + 8 = 13$. The $3$ is the difference between the days, a different question.

problems.prompt: A picture graph draws its rows starting at different places. This makes it:
options: misleading, even if the counts are right
problems.explanation: The reader compares LENGTHS, so a row starting further along looks bigger than it is. Every count could be correct and the picture still lie.

problems.prompt: Row A has $9$ pictures and row B has $9$ pictures, but row B starts further right. The counts are:
problems.explanation: The counts are both $9$: $9 - 9 = 0$ difference. Only the drawing is unfair, which is exactly why the starting line matters.

steps.title: The unfair graph
steps.prompt: Two rows both hold $9$ pictures, but one starts further right and looks longer. What is wrong?
options: the rows do not start from the same line
steps.explanation: Both counts are $9$, so the difference is $9 - 9 = 0$. The rows only LOOK different because they begin in different places — the counts are honest and the drawing is not.

steps.title: What you learned
points: One picture stands for one thing, so a row's length IS its count.
Compare rows by their gap: $6$ horses against $4$ sheep is $6 - 4 = 2$ more.
Add the rows for the total: $6 + 4 + 3 = 13$.
Every row must start from the same line, or the picture misleads even with correct counts.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Before answering anything from a picture graph, check the rows all begin at the same left-hand line. A graph that fails that test cannot be trusted, however carefully its pictures were drawn.

steps.title: Chapter practice
steps.intro: Gap for "how many more", sum for "altogether".

problems.prompt: Rows of $7$ and $2$: how many more in the longer row?
problems.explanation: $7 - 2 = 5$ more. The $9$ adds the rows and the $7$ just repeats the longer one.

problems.prompt: Rows of $6$, $3$ and $5$ hold altogether:
problems.explanation: $6 + 3 = 9$, then $9 + 5 = 14$ things drawn in all.

problems.prompt: In a one-for-one graph, the row with the most pictures is:
options: impossible to know without a key
problems.explanation: One picture per thing means there is no key to apply — the longest row simply is the biggest count.

steps.title: You've finished "Picture Graphs"
steps.body: Drawing a count turns a comparison into something you can see. The next lesson swaps the little pictures for plain blocks, which are quicker to draw and just as honest — as long as one block still means one thing.

lessons.title: Block Graphs
lessons.concreteComparison: Drawing twelve little goats takes a while, and the goats were never the point — their number was. A block graph replaces each picture with a plain square, and nothing at all is lost.
lessons.objective: Draw and read a block graph where one block stands for one thing, compare bars, and say what makes a block graph trustworthy.
concept: **One block stands for one thing.** A bar of $9$ blocks means $9$ things counted. It is a picture graph with the drawing simplified away, and the counting rule is exactly the same.

**Every block must be the same size.** If one bar's blocks are drawn larger, its bar looks bigger than its count deserves. Equal blocks, all starting from the same line, is what makes the comparison fair.

**Equal counts must make equal bars.** If two days both had $7$ visitors, their bars are exactly as tall as each other — $7 - 7 = 0$ difference, and the graph should show none. A graph that shows a gap where there is none is wrong, however neat it looks.
lessons.keyIdea: A block graph is a picture graph with plain blocks: one block per thing, all blocks the same size, all bars from the same line.

facts.title: Reading a bar
facts.explanation: A bar of 9 blocks stands 5 blocks above a bar of 4.

facts.title: Equal counts, equal bars
facts.explanation: Two counts of 7 must produce bars of exactly the same height.

workedExamples.statement: A block graph shows red $6$, blue $9$, green $4$. Which is tallest, and how far does it stand above the shortest?
workedExamples.solution: Blue is tallest at $9$ blocks, and green is shortest at $4$. Blue stands $9 - 4 = 5$ blocks above green, which is $5$ more things counted — one block, one thing.

workedExamples.statement: Monday and Tuesday both had $7$ visitors, but Monday's bar is drawn taller. What is wrong?
workedExamples.note: Equal counts must give equal bars.
workedExamples.solution: The counts are the same, so the difference is $7 - 7 = 0$ and the bars must match exactly. Monday's bar being taller means its blocks were drawn larger, or it did not start from the same line — the graph is misleading even though both counts are right.

commonMistakes.text: Drawing blocks of different sizes in different bars.
commonMistakes.correction: The reader compares bar heights, so unequal blocks make the comparison false. Every block must be the same size and every bar must start from the same line.

commonMistakes.text: Counting the bars instead of the blocks — reading a three-bar graph as "3".
commonMistakes.correction: The bars name the things being counted; the blocks are the count. Three bars of 6, 9 and 4 hold 6 + 9 + 4 = 19 things.

tryIt.statement: Bars of $8$ and $5$ blocks. How much taller is the first, and how many things in total?
tryIt.solution: Taller by $8 - 5 = 3$ blocks, which is $3$ more things. Together they hold $8 + 5 = 13$.

tryIt.statement: Why must every block in a block graph be the same size?
tryIt.solution: Because the reader compares bar HEIGHTS. Larger blocks in one bar make it stand taller than its count deserves, so a bar of $4$ could out-tower a bar of $6$ even though $6 > 4$.

steps.title: Blocks instead of pictures
beats: Drawing twelve little goats is slow, and the goats were never the point — the number was. So replace each picture with a plain block.
The graph below shows red $6$, blue $9$, green $4$, one block per thing. Nothing has been lost: blue is still visibly the tallest.
Blue stands $9 - 4 = 5$ blocks above green, and that is $5$ more things counted. One block, one thing — the same rule as a picture graph, drawn faster.

steps.title: Read the bars
steps.intro: Count the blocks, not the bars.

examples.prompt: Red $6$, blue $9$, green $4$. Which is tallest, and by how much over green?
steps: Blue at $9$ blocks is tallest; green at $4$ is shortest.

examples.prompt: Red $6$, blue $9$, green $4$. How many things altogether?

steps.title: Read the block graph
steps.intro: One block is one thing.

problems.prompt: From the graph below, how much taller is blue than red?
problems.explanation: Blue $9$, red $6$: $9 - 6 = 3$ blocks taller, meaning three more things. The $15$ adds the bars instead of comparing them.

problems.prompt: A three-bar graph with bars of $6$, $9$ and $4$ shows how many things?
problems.explanation: The bars name the categories; the blocks are the count: $6 + 9 + 4 = 19$. Answering $3$ counts the bars.

problems.prompt: A bar of $7$ blocks stands for:
problems.explanation: One block per thing, so seven blocks is seven things — no key and no multiplying.

steps.title: Bars against blocks
steps.prompt: A graph has $3$ bars holding $6$, $9$ and $4$ blocks. How many things were counted?
steps.explanation: The bars are the categories and the blocks are the count: $6 + 9 + 4 = 19$ things. Answering $3$ counts the bars and $9$ takes only the tallest.

steps.title: Squared paper was invented for this
steps.body: The reason exercise books come with squares printed on them is largely to make graphs like this honest. Every square is identical, so a bar of nine squares cannot accidentally be drawn taller than it should — the paper enforces the fairness that the drawer might forget.

steps.title: What makes a block graph fair
beats: Two rules keep a block graph honest, and both are about the DRAWING rather than the counting.
First, every block must be the same size. Second, every bar must start from the same line. Break either and a bar of $4$ can be made to tower over a bar of $6$, even though $6 > 4$.

The graph below shows Monday $7$ and Tuesday $7$. The counts are identical, so $7 - 7 = 0$ — the bars must be exactly as tall as each other. A graph showing a gap here would be wrong however neatly it was drawn.

steps.title: Fair or unfair?
steps.intro: Same blocks, same starting line.

examples.prompt: Monday $7$, Tuesday $7$, but Monday's bar is taller. What is wrong?
steps: So the bars must match. Monday's blocks were drawn larger, or its bar started higher — the drawing is wrong, not the count.

examples.prompt: Why must all bars start from the same line?
steps: Readers compare bar heights, not their tops.
A bar starting higher looks bigger than its count: a bar of $4$ could seem to beat one of $6$, though $6 > 4$.

steps.title: Is the graph honest?
steps.intro: Check the blocks and the baseline.

problems.prompt: Two bars both hold $7$ blocks but one is drawn taller. This graph is:
options: misleading — equal counts need equal bars
fine, if the counts are right
showing that one really is bigger
problems.explanation: $7 - 7 = 0$, so the bars must be identical. A visible gap where the counts agree means the drawing is at fault.

problems.prompt: One bar's blocks are drawn twice the size of another's. The graph:
options: is fine as long as the counts are labelled
problems.explanation: The reader compares heights, so double-size blocks double a bar's apparent count. Labels do not undo a picture that lies.

problems.prompt: A fair block graph needs:
options: equal blocks and one starting line
the tallest bar on the left
problems.explanation: Those two rules are what make bar heights match counts. The order of the bars and how many there are is up to you.

steps.title: The rule that keeps it honest
steps.prompt: Why must every block be the same size?
options: so a bar's height matches its count
so the bars fit on the page
so each bar has the same number of blocks
steps.explanation: Readers judge by height, so unequal blocks break the link between height and count — a bar of $4$ with big blocks could out-tower a bar of $6$, though $6 - 4 = 2$ says the opposite.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A block graph is a picture graph with plain blocks: one block per thing.
Compare bars by their gap: $9 - 4 = 5$ blocks is $5$ more things.
Every block must be the same size and every bar must start from the same line.
Equal counts must give equal bars — $7 - 7 = 0$ means no visible gap.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Draw block graphs on squared paper and use one printed square per block. The paper then guarantees the fairness for you, and there is nothing left to get wrong except the counting.

steps.title: Chapter practice
steps.intro: Blocks are the count; bars are the categories.

problems.prompt: Bars of $5$ and $9$ blocks: the taller stands above the shorter by:
problems.explanation: $9 - 5 = 4$ blocks, meaning four more things counted.

problems.prompt: Four bars of $3$, $6$, $2$ and $5$ blocks hold:
problems.explanation: $3 + 6 = 9$, $9 + 2 = 11$, $11 + 5 = 16$ things in all. Answering $4$ counts the bars.

problems.prompt: Two counts of $6$ should be drawn as:
options: two bars of exactly the same height
problems.explanation: Equal counts must give equal bars: $6 - 6 = 0$ difference, so no visible gap.

steps.title: You've finished "Block Graphs"
steps.body: You can now draw a count so that it can be seen and trusted. The last lesson of the year stops drawing and starts asking — because a graph is only useful once you know what questions it can answer.

lessons.title: Answering Questions from Data
lessons.concreteComparison: A finished graph is not the end of the work — it is the beginning. Which sport was most popular? How many more chose wrestling than archery? How many children were asked altogether? Every one of those is answered by reading the same three bars a different way.
lessons.objective: Answer most, fewest, how-many-more and how-many-altogether questions from a graph, and say which arithmetic each question needs.
concept: **Most and fewest need no arithmetic at all.** The tallest bar is the most popular and the shortest is the least. With wrestling $9$, archery $5$ and racing $6$, wrestling wins and archery comes last — read straight off the picture.
**"How many more" is a subtraction.** Wrestling over archery is $9 - 5 = 4$. The answer is the GAP between two bars, never the height of the taller one.
**"How many altogether" is an addition.** All three bars together: $9 + 5 + 6 = 20$ children asked. Different question, different operation — and reading which is which is the real skill.
lessons.keyIdea: Most and fewest are read off; "how many more" subtracts two bars; "how many altogether" adds them all.

facts.title: How many more
facts.explanation: The gap between the wrestling and archery bars.

facts.title: How many altogether
facts.explanation: All three bars added gives everyone who was asked.

workedExamples.statement: A graph shows wrestling $9$, archery $5$, racing $6$. Name the most and least popular, and say how many more chose wrestling than archery.
workedExamples.solution: Most popular: wrestling, the tallest bar at $9$. Least: archery at $5$. More for wrestling than archery: $9 - 5 = 4$ children — the gap between the bars, not the height of either.

workedExamples.statement: From the same graph, how many children were asked altogether?
workedExamples.note: Every child chose exactly one sport.
workedExamples.solution: Each child appears in exactly one bar, so adding the bars counts everyone: $9 + 5 + 6 = 20$ children. Note this is an addition, while the previous question was a subtraction — the words decide.

commonMistakes.text: Answering "how many more chose wrestling than archery" with 9.
commonMistakes.correction: 9 is how many chose wrestling. The question asks for the GAP: 9 − 5 = 4. Read what is being compared before you answer.

commonMistakes.text: Adding bars to answer a comparison question, or subtracting to answer a total.
commonMistakes.correction: "How many more" subtracts two bars; "how many altogether" adds them all. The words choose the operation, not the numbers.

tryIt.statement: From wrestling $9$, archery $5$, racing $6$: how many more chose racing than archery?
tryIt.solution: The gap between the two bars: $6 - 5 = 1$ child.

tryIt.statement: A graph shows boys $8$ and girls $11$. How many children altogether, and how many more girls?

steps.title: Reading most and fewest
beats: The graph below shows what a class chose: wrestling $9$, archery $5$, racing $6$.
"Which was most popular?" needs no arithmetic — the tallest bar answers it. Wrestling, at $9$, since $9 > 6$ and $9 > 5$.
"Which was least?" is the shortest bar: archery at $5$. Two questions answered by looking, which is exactly why the data was drawn.

steps.title: Most and fewest
steps.intro: Read the tallest and shortest bars.

examples.prompt: Wrestling $9$, archery $5$, racing $6$. Which is most popular?
steps: The tallest bar is wrestling at $9$.

examples.prompt: Which was least popular?
steps: The shortest bar is archery at $5$.

steps.title: Read it off
steps.intro: Tallest is most; shortest is fewest.

problems.prompt: From the graph below, the least popular sport is:
problems.explanation: Archery's bar is shortest at $5$, below racing's $6$ and wrestling's $9$.

problems.prompt: With bars of $8$, $11$ and $4$, the most popular has:
problems.explanation: The tallest bar is $11$, since $11 > 8 > 4$. The $23$ adds all three bars, which answers a total instead.

problems.prompt: Answering "which is most popular" requires:
options: subtracting the smallest from the largest
problems.explanation: The tallest bar answers it directly. Adding and subtracting answer the total and the gap, which are different questions.

steps.title: Which question needs no sum?
steps.prompt: Which of these can be answered just by looking at the bars?
options: how many more chose wrestling than archery
how many children were asked altogether
steps.explanation: The tallest bar names the most popular with no arithmetic. The other two need $9 - 5 = 4$ and $9 + 5 + 6 = 20$ respectively.

steps.title: The question comes before the graph
steps.body: Real surveys are designed backwards: someone decides what they need to know, and only then chooses what to count. A graph that answers no question anyone asked is a common and expensive mistake — which is why this lesson matters more than the drawing did.

steps.title: How many more, and how many altogether
beats: The two remaining questions each need a sum, and the words tell you which.
"How many more chose wrestling than archery?" asks for the GAP between two bars: $9 - 5 = 4$ children. Not $9$ — that is simply how many chose wrestling.

"How many children were asked altogether?" adds every bar: $9 + 5 + 6 = 20$. The graph below shows a two-bar version — boys $8$, girls $11$ — where the same two questions give $11 - 8 = 3$ and $8 + 11 = 19$.

steps.title: Choose the operation
steps.intro: "More" subtracts; "altogether" adds.

examples.prompt: How many more chose wrestling ($9$) than archery ($5$)?
steps: "How many more" asks for the gap.

examples.prompt: How many children were asked altogether, from bars of $9$, $5$ and $6$?
steps: Each child is in exactly one bar.

steps.title: Which sum?
steps.intro: Read the words, then choose.

problems.prompt: Boys $8$, girls $11$. How many more girls than boys?
problems.explanation: "How many more" is the gap: $11 - 8 = 3$. The $19$ adds them and $11$ just repeats the taller bar.

problems.prompt: Boys $8$, girls $11$. How many children altogether?
problems.explanation: "Altogether" adds every bar: $8 + 11 = 19$ children.

problems.prompt: Wrestling $9$, archery $5$, racing $6$. How many more chose racing than archery?
problems.explanation: The gap between those two bars: $6 - 5 = 1$ child. Adding them gives $11$, and $6$ is just racing's count.

steps.title: Reading the question
steps.prompt: "How many more chose wrestling ($9$) than archery ($5$)?" The answer is:
steps.explanation: The question asks for the GAP between the two bars: $9 - 5 = 4$ children, with receipt $5 + 4 = 9$ ✓. Answering $9$ gives wrestling's count and $14$ adds the two bars together.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Most and fewest are read straight off — the tallest and shortest bars.
"How many more" subtracts two bars: $9 - 5 = 4$.
"How many altogether" adds every bar: $9 + 5 + 6 = 20$.
The words of the question choose the operation, not the numbers in the graph.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Underline the question's key words before you look at the graph — "most", "more than", "altogether". The operation is decided by those words, and deciding it first stops the numbers from tempting you into the wrong one.

steps.title: Chapter practice
steps.intro: Words first, then the arithmetic.

problems.prompt: Bars of $7$, $4$ and $9$. How many altogether?
problems.explanation: $7 + 4 = 11$, then $11 + 9 = 20$. The $5$ is the gap between the tallest and shortest.

problems.prompt: Bars of $7$ and $4$. How many more in the taller?
problems.explanation: $7 - 4 = 3$ more. Adding gives $11$ and $7$ just repeats the taller bar.

problems.prompt: Which question needs an ADDITION?
problems.explanation: "Altogether" adds every bar. "How many more" subtracts two, and "most popular" needs no arithmetic at all.

steps.title: You've finished "Answering Questions from Data" — and the Grade 3 year
steps.body: Tallies, tables, picture graphs, block graphs and the questions they answer. And with them the whole year: numbers to a thousand, adding and subtracting them, multiplying and dividing, fractions, shapes, measuring, and now data. Everything here is waiting for you again next year, one size larger.

practice.statement: Read the tally shown, and say how many bundles and singles it holds.
practice.solution: Two bundles and three singles: $2 \times 5 = 10$ from the bundles, plus $3$, giving $10 + 3 = 13$. Three is less than five, as the leftovers always must be.

practice.statement: Draw $18$ as tally marks. How many bundles, how many singles, and how do you know no more bundles are possible?
practice.solution: Three bundles use $3 \times 5 = 15$ marks, leaving $18 - 15 = 3$ singles. No fourth bundle is possible because only $3$ marks remain and a bundle needs $5$ — and $3 < 5$.

practice.statement: A table reads sheep $9$, goats $6$, horses $4$. Give the total, the most numerous animal, and the gap between the largest and smallest rows.
practice.solution: Total: $9 + 6 + 4 = 19$ animals. Most numerous: sheep at $9$. Gap between largest and smallest: $9 - 4 = 5$.

practice.statement: A table has rows of $12$ and $7$ and a total of $25$. Find the missing row and prove it.
practice.solution: The known rows come to $12 + 7 = 19$, so the missing row is $25 - 19 = 6$. Proof: $19 + 6 = 25$ ✓, matching the written total.

practice.statement: Explain why every row of a picture graph must begin at the same line, using two rows of equal count as your example.
practice.solution: The reader compares row LENGTHS, so the starting point decides what the length looks like. Two rows both holding $9$ pictures have a difference of $9 - 9 = 0$ and must look identical; if one begins further along it appears larger, and the picture lies even though both counts are correct.

practice.statement: From the graph shown, answer all three: which sport was most popular, how many more chose wrestling than archery, and how many children were asked.
practice.solution: Most popular: wrestling, the tallest bar at $9$. More for wrestling than archery: $9 - 5 = 4$ children. Asked altogether: $9 + 5 + 6 = 20$. Three questions, three different operations — none, a subtraction, and an addition.

practice.statement: A block graph draws one bar with blocks twice the size of another's. Explain what goes wrong even if both counts are correct.
practice.solution: Readers judge a bar by its height, and double-size blocks double the height a count produces. A bar of $4$ drawn with big blocks can stand taller than a bar of $6$ drawn with small ones, reversing the true comparison — $6 > 4$, with a real gap of $6 - 4 = 2$ in the other direction.

practice.statement: Bat is asked how many more children chose racing ($6$) than archery ($5$) and answers $6$. Name his mistake and give the right answer.
practice.solution: He gave racing's count instead of the gap between the two bars. "How many more" is a subtraction: $6 - 5 = 1$ child, with receipt $5 + 1 = 6$ ✓. His $6$ answers "how many chose racing", which was not the question.

testYourself.statement: A tally shows three bundles and four singles. Give the count, and explain why four is the largest number of singles possible.
testYourself.solution: Three bundles are $3 \times 5 = 15$, plus $4$ singles: $15 + 4 = 19$. Four is the maximum because a fifth single would be laid across the other four and close a new bundle — so the leftovers are always fewer than five, and $4 < 5$.

testYourself.statement: A table reads red $8$, blue $5$, green $7$, with a total written as $21$. Check the total and say whether the table is consistent.
testYourself.solution: The rows add to $8 + 5 = 13$, then $13 + 7 = 20$. The written total of $21$ is one too many — $21 - 20 = 1$ — so the table is not consistent, and either a row or the total was recorded wrongly. This is exactly the error a written total exists to catch.

testYourself.statement: A one-for-one picture graph shows $7$ birds, $3$ fish and $5$ insects. Answer: most common, how many more birds than fish, and how many creatures in all.
testYourself.solution: Most common: birds, the longest row at $7$. More birds than fish: $7 - 3 = 4$. Creatures in all: $7 + 3 + 5 = 15$.

testYourself.statement: Two block graph bars each hold $6$ blocks, but one is drawn taller. Say what has gone wrong and what the true comparison is.
testYourself.solution: The counts are equal, so the true difference is $6 - 6 = 0$ and the bars must be exactly the same height. One bar's blocks were drawn larger, or it did not start from the same baseline — the drawing is at fault, not the counting.

testYourself.statement: From bars of wrestling $9$, archery $5$ and racing $6$, write one question answered by adding and one answered by subtracting, and answer both.
testYourself.solution: Adding: "How many children were asked altogether?" — $9 + 5 + 6 = 20$. Subtracting: "How many more chose wrestling than archery?" — $9 - 5 = 4$. The words of a question choose its operation, and the same three bars serve both.

testYourself.statement: A survey records $12$ children choosing wrestling as two bundles and two singles in a tally, then draws it as a bar of $12$ blocks. Follow the count through all three forms and say what each form is good at.
testYourself.solution: The tally reads $2 \times 5 + 2 = 12$ — good for recording while the counting is still happening. The table row reads $12$ — good for comparing with other rows and for totalling. The bar of $12$ blocks — good for seeing the comparison without reading any number at all. The count never changed through any of it: $12$ throughout.
